body:
Gujarat's nuclear-power installation

Kakrapar Atomic Power Station (KAPS) is a nuclear electricity-generating installation in Surat district, Gujarat. It is situated near Kakrapar on the Tapi River in southern Gujarat. The station is operated by the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL), a public-sector enterprise under the Department of Atomic Energy.

Kakrapar is an important example of the application of nuclear science to electricity generation in India. Unlike a research laboratory, which conducts experiments, a nuclear power station uses energy released from controlled nuclear reactions to produce electricity for the power system.

Location: Kakrapar Atomic Power Station is in Surat district, Gujarat, beside the Tapi River. The river's name should not be confused with the neighbouring Tapi district.

Why nuclear energy is used for electricity

Energy is stored in the nucleus of an atom. In a nuclear power reactor, a controlled process called nuclear fission releases part of this energy as heat. The heat is used to produce steam, which drives a turbine connected to an electricity generator.

Nuclear electricity differs from electricity generated by burning coal or natural gas. A nuclear reactor obtains its heat from changes in atomic nuclei rather than from combustion. Consequently, the reactor does not need to burn fossil fuel to produce heat. Nuclear power has relatively low greenhouse-gas emissions during electricity generation, although its complete life cycle includes emissions from mining, construction and other activities.

Nuclear energy is generally classified as a non-renewable energy source because the uranium used as fuel is a finite mineral resource. It should not be confused with solar or wind energy, which depend on naturally replenished energy flows.

Why the Gujarat location matters

There are 2 separate geographical relationships to remember. First, Kakrapar is a nuclear-power site situated beside the Tapi River. Second, nuclear-emergency planning concerns surrounding settlements and administrative areas, not merely the district in which the reactors stand.

An emergency affecting the public would require coordination between the nuclear installation and the relevant district authorities. Gujarat's disaster-management arrangements therefore consider the surrounding region, including Surat and Tapi districts, where appropriate.

Different nuclear activities are not the same

Nuclear science supports electricity generation, fuel production, radiation monitoring, research and other applications. These activities may be carried out by different institutions. The presence of a nuclear-related institution in Gujarat does not necessarily mean that it generates nuclear electricity.

For example, Kakrapar generates electricity, the Heavy Water Plant at Hazira is associated with a material used in certain reactors, and the Institute for Plasma Research near Gandhinagar conducts plasma and fusion research. Their functions must be distinguished.

Prelims focus

  • Kakrapar Atomic Power Station is located in Surat district, Gujarat.
  • The station is situated beside the Tapi River.
  • NPCIL operates Kakrapar's nuclear-power reactors.
  • Nuclear electricity is generated using heat from controlled nuclear fission.
  • Trap: The Tapi River's name does not place Kakrapar Atomic Power Station in Tapi district.

[Sources: Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Kakrapar Atomic Power Station, Operating Performance, location and reactor details, consulted 16 November 2026; NPCIL, Kakrapar Gujarat Site: An Introduction, section 1.1, p. 5, 2021; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Action Plan for Nuclear & Radiological Disaster, introductory section, consulted 16 November 2026; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed p. 82.]

body:
The four generating units

Kakrapar has 4 commercial nuclear-power reactor units. All 4 are Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs). The first 2 units have an electrical capacity of 220 MWe each, while Units 3 and 4 have an electrical capacity of 700 MWe each.

The abbreviation MWe means megawatts of electrical capacity. It describes the capacity to generate electricity, not the total quantity of electricity produced over a month or year. Actual electricity generation depends on operating conditions, maintenance and other factors.

Reactor unitElectrical capacityCommercial operation began
KAPS Unit 1220 MWe6 May 1993
KAPS Unit 2220 MWe1 September 1995
KAPS Unit 3700 MWe30 June 2023
KAPS Unit 4700 MWe31 March 2024

The combined installed electrical capacity of the 4 units is:

\(2\times220+2\times700=1840\ \text{MWe}\)

Thus, the 2 original units contribute 440 MWe, and Units 3 and 4 contribute 1,400 MWe. The newer pair accounts for approximately 76% of the station's installed electrical capacity.

The significance of Units 3 and 4

Kakrapar Units 3 and 4 form India's first pair of indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs. Their development represents the adoption of a larger Indian-designed reactor capacity after earlier PHWR units of smaller capacities.

The word indigenous refers to the domestic development of the reactor technology. It does not mean that every material or component must necessarily originate from the same location or that a particular nuclear fuel has unlimited domestic availability.

Commercial operation is a specific milestone

A reactor passes through several stages before commercial operation. These stages have different meanings:

  1. First criticality: the controlled nuclear chain reaction becomes self-sustaining.
  2. First grid synchronisation: the generating unit is connected to the electricity grid for the first time.
  3. Commercial operation: the unit is formally placed into commercial generating service after the applicable commissioning process.
  4. Full-power operation: the unit operates at its authorised full-power level, subject to the relevant permissions and operating conditions.

These milestones need not occur on the same date. In particular, a unit can begin commercial operation before subsequently achieving full-power operation.

Operating status at the content cutoff

Content cutoff: 16 November 2026. NPCIL's Kakrapar operating-performance page lists all 4 reactors as operating units and reports generation statistics for April–August 2026 of financial year 2026–27. Its confirmed commercial-operation dates are those shown in the table above.

Older project pages and construction reports may still describe Units 3 and 4 as projects under construction. Such descriptions represent an earlier stage and should not replace the later operating-status information.

Prelims focus

  • Kakrapar has 4 PHWR units with a combined capacity of 1,840 MWe.
  • Units 1 and 2 have capacities of 220 MWe each.
  • Units 3 and 4 have capacities of 700 MWe each.
  • Unit 3 began commercial operation in 2023; Unit 4 in 2024.
  • Units 3 and 4 are India's first pair of indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs.
  • Trap: First criticality, grid synchronisation, commercial operation and full-power operation are different milestones.

[Sources: NPCIL, Kakrapar Atomic Power Station, Operating Performance, unit capacities, commercial-operation dates and April–August 2026 generation statistics, consulted 16 November 2026; NPCIL, Directors' Report, Annual Report 2023–24, section Kakrapar Atomic Power Project 3&4; NPCIL, Kakrapar Atomic Power Project 3&4, Chapter 2: Project Profile, section 2.1, p. 2-2.]

body:
Controlled nuclear fission

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus into lighter nuclei, accompanied by the release of energy and neutrons. In a nuclear reactor, the fission process is maintained as a controlled chain reaction so that heat is produced at a manageable rate.

Natural uranium contains different uranium isotopes. Uranium-235 is the isotope that readily undergoes fission with slow neutrons, while uranium-238 makes up most of natural uranium. In a pressurised heavy-water reactor, the use of heavy water helps make it possible to use natural uranium fuel.

Kakrapar's 700 MWe PHWR units use natural uranium dioxide as nuclear fuel. Uranium dioxide is a fuel material; it is not the same substance as the heavy water used within the reactor system.

The basic electricity-generation process

  1. Fission releases heat: controlled nuclear reactions in the fuel produce thermal energy.
  2. Heat is transferred: the reactor's cooling system removes heat from the fuel and transfers it for steam production.
  3. Steam drives a turbine: thermal energy is converted into mechanical rotation.
  4. The generator produces electricity: the rotating turbine drives an electrical generator.

The principle of driving a turbine-generator with steam is also found in fossil-fuel thermal power stations. The important difference is the source of heat: nuclear fission in a nuclear station and fuel combustion in a coal- or gas-fired station.

What heavy water does

Heavy water is water containing deuterium, a heavier isotope of hydrogen. Its chemical formula is D2O.

Heavy water has 2 important functions in a PHWR:

  • Moderator: it slows down neutrons so that they can more effectively sustain the intended fission chain reaction in the fuel.
  • Coolant: it carries heat away from the reactor fuel in the cooling system.

The same substance can perform different physical functions, but heavy water is not the uranium fuel. Heavy water does not replace the need for fissile material in the reactor.

Uranium and thorium are not interchangeable

Uranium and thorium are both associated with nuclear energy, but their roles are different. Naturally occurring uranium contains uranium-235, which can sustain fission under suitable reactor conditions. Thorium-232 is primarily a fertile material: through neutron absorption and subsequent nuclear transformations, it can be used to produce uranium-233, which is fissile.

India's interest in thorium arises partly from the occurrence of thorium-bearing mineral sands along parts of its coastline. This broader fuel-resource context does not mean that Kakrapar's current PHWR units directly use thorium as their ordinary fuel.

Fuel releases energy; the moderator influences neutron behaviour; the coolant removes heat. These functions should not be confused simply because they operate together inside a nuclear-power system.

What happens when the reactor is shut down

Stopping the sustained fission chain reaction does not make all heat disappear immediately. Radioactive fission products continue to release decay heat. Therefore, safe shutdown also requires appropriate cooling and monitoring. This is one reason nuclear safety includes backup cooling arrangements as well as reactor shutdown systems.

Prelims focus

  • PHWR stands for Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor.
  • Kakrapar's PHWR units use uranium-based nuclear fuel.
  • D2O is heavy water; it serves as a moderator and coolant.
  • Fission heat ultimately drives a turbine and electricity generator.
  • Thorium-232 is primarily fertile; it is not equivalent to ready-to-use uranium-235 fuel.
  • Trap: Reactor shutdown does not immediately eliminate decay heat or the need for cooling.

[Sources: NPCIL and National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Environmental Impact Assessment Report for Kakrapar Atomic Power Project 3&4, October 2006, Chapter 2, section 2.1, p. 2-2; Heavy Water Board, Function and Duties, Heavy Water Plant Hazira, consulted 16 November 2026; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 34–35.]

title: How Kakrapar's pressurised heavy-water reactors produce electricity

body:
A nuclear-power station is part of a larger system

Generating electricity is only one stage of the nuclear-energy system. Nuclear fuel must be obtained from suitable minerals, processed and fabricated before it can be used in a reactor. Other institutions produce supporting materials, carry out scientific research and monitor environmental safety.

This wider system is often called the nuclear fuel cycle. At an elementary level, its important activities include obtaining uranium, preparing reactor fuel, using the fuel to generate energy and managing radioactive materials after use.

Gujarat's heavy-water connection

The Heavy Water Plant at Hazira, in Surat district, is a unit of the Heavy Water Board (HWB) under the Department of Atomic Energy. It is integrated with the KRIBHCO fertiliser complex at Hazira.

The Hazira plant was commissioned in January 1991. Its principal function is the production of heavy water, D2O, which is used in nuclear-power and research reactors. Heavy-water production is a chemical-industrial activity; it should not be mistaken for the generation of nuclear electricity.

Hazira produces heavy water; Kakrapar produces nuclear electricity. The 2 sites have different roles even though both are connected with India's nuclear-energy programme.

Where nuclear fuel is prepared

The Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC) at Hyderabad, Telangana, is a Department of Atomic Energy industrial organisation that manufactures fuel bundles and components for nuclear reactors, including PHWRs.

The uranium needed for nuclear fuel originates from mineral resources rather than from the heavy-water plant. Important Indian uranium-resource areas include the Singhbhum region of Jharkhand and deposits in parts of Rajasthan. Thorium-bearing monazite sands occur along parts of the Indian coast, notably in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

These resource locations should be distinguished from the location of the power station. Kakrapar's presence in Gujarat does not mean Gujarat must be the source of its uranium ore.

Research and monitoring institutions

The Institute for Plasma Research (IPR) near Gandhinagar is an aided research institute of the Department of Atomic Energy. It studies plasma physics, magnetic confinement and technologies connected with nuclear-fusion research and other plasma applications.

A plasma is an ionised state of matter containing charged particles. Nuclear-fusion research investigates conditions under which light atomic nuclei can combine and release energy. This is fundamentally different from the fission reactions used to generate electricity at Kakrapar.

The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) also performs important nuclear research and environmental-monitoring functions. Environmental Survey Laboratories associated with nuclear-power sites examine environmental samples to support independent radiological surveillance.

Institution or facilityLocationMain function
Kakrapar Atomic Power StationSurat district, GujaratCommercial nuclear electricity generation
Heavy Water PlantHazira, GujaratHeavy-water production
Nuclear Fuel ComplexHyderabad, TelanganaNuclear fuel fabrication
Institute for Plasma ResearchNear Gandhinagar, GujaratPlasma and fusion research
Environmental Survey LaboratoryKakrapar siteEnvironmental radiation surveillance

How the activities are related

Uranium resources and nuclear-fuel fabrication are connected with the supply of reactor fuel. Heavy-water production supports reactors that require heavy water. Nuclear-power stations use fuel and reactor systems to produce electricity. Environmental laboratories examine possible radiological effects around operating installations.

Plasma and fusion research is a related field of nuclear science, but it is not an operational stage in Kakrapar's uranium-fission electricity-generation process.

Prelims focus

  • HWP Hazira is under the Heavy Water Board and was commissioned in January 1991.
  • The Hazira plant is integrated with the KRIBHCO fertiliser complex.
  • NFC Hyderabad fabricates nuclear fuel for reactors.
  • IPR near Gandhinagar conducts plasma and fusion research.
  • BARC Environmental Survey Laboratories support environmental radiation monitoring.
  • Trap: A heavy-water plant or fusion-research institute is not the same as a commercial nuclear-power station.

[Sources: Heavy Water Board, About HWP Hazira and Function and Duties Hazira, consulted 16 November 2026; Nuclear Fuel Complex, Overview, Hyderabad, consulted 16 November 2026; Institute for Plasma Research, About the Institute and Research Activities, consulted 16 November 2026; Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Radiation Safety for Protecting the Environment, environmental surveillance section, consulted 16 November 2026; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 80–82.]
